newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Meinl pays higher dividend, sees sales up.
newsitem.headline: Meinl pays higher dividend, sees sales up.

text.p: Hungarian retail group Csemege-Julius Meinl will pay a 14 percent dividend on its 1996 earnings, as against 13 percent last year, following shareholders' approval on Thursday.
The company, which is more than 90 percent owned by Austria's Meinl group, set November 30 as the latest date for dividend payouts despite small shareholders' attempts to bring the deadline forward.
The group posted an after-tax profit of 852.5 million forints on net sales revenues of 45.2 billion forints in 1996.
President and CEO Zoltan Hazi told shareholders the group boosted its market share by 0.4 percentage points to 5.4 percent despite a more difficult operating enviroment.
"Trading was characterised by a significant price competition," Hazi said, adding that food retail seemed to have faced the stiffest competition.

In addition to its traditional food shops, Julius Meinl operates discount and cash-and-carry outlets, with the latter accounting for an increasing part within total sales and thus reducing margins through lower retail prices.

"Our margins are seen shrinking by 2.1 percent (in 1997), reflecting both the lessening of the inflationary impact on prices and the increasing proportion within turnover of discount and C+C chains." Csemege-Julius Meinl said in its 1997 business plans.
Hazi said the 1997 sales revenue target was 63 billion forints, with a planned 1997 profit in excess of last year's and a further rise in its market share.
"The most important target remains increasing market share...and opening outlets in new shopping centres," Hazi said.
"Further investments make the increase in sales revenues a realistic target," the plan added.
In 1996 capital expenditure amounted to 2.3 billion forints, as against 1.9 billion in 1995.
